14960:
A sphincter is a ring-shaped muscle that wraps around an opening or passage in the body, and whose job is to open and close that passage on cue — like a biological valve or drawstring. It is found throughout the human body (and in animals too), wherever a tube or hollow organ needs a controlled gateway.

The word is used as a medical and anatomical term. When doctors, biologists, or anyone in healthcare refers to a sphincter, they mean this specific type of circular muscle that acts as a gate.

Picture a garden hose with a rubber band wrapped tightly around the middle. When the rubber band squeezes, nothing flows through. When it loosens, flow resumes. A sphincter works in exactly this way, except it is alive and responsive.

  • When a sphincter contracts (tightens), it closes the passage — nothing gets through.
  • When a sphincter relaxes (loosens), it opens the passage — contents can flow through.

This simple squeeze-and-release action is the entire mechanical principle behind every sphincter in your body.

Not all sphincters behave the same way in terms of your control over them.

Voluntary sphincters are ones you can consciously control. You decide when to open or close them. The classic example is the external anal sphincter — the muscle that lets you choose when to have a bowel movement. You are using conscious control when you "hold it" until you reach a toilet.

Involuntary sphincters operate entirely on their own, controlled by your nervous system automatically, without any conscious thought or effort from you. These work behind the scenes 24 hours a day. You cannot consciously command them to open or close. Most sphincters in your body belong to this category.

Some sphincters have both a voluntary and an involuntary component working together — one layer you control, one layer that works automatically.
Where Sphincters Are Found in the Body

The human body has many sphincters, scattered across multiple organ systems. Here are the most important ones:

1. Digestive System

The digestive tract is essentially a long tube from your mouth to your anus, and it has multiple sphincters along the way acting as checkpoint gates.

Lower Esophageal Sphincter (also called the Cardiac Sphincter)
Located where your esophagus (food pipe) meets your stomach. After you swallow food and it travels down into the stomach, this sphincter closes tightly to stop stomach acid from traveling back up. If this sphincter is weak or faulty, acid splashes back into the esophagus — this is exactly what causes acid reflux and the burning sensation known as heartburn.

Pyloric Sphincter
Located at the bottom of the stomach, where the stomach connects to the small intestine (specifically the first section called the duodenum). Food doesn't dump out of your stomach all at once. This sphincter controls how gradually the partially digested food (now a mushy liquid called chyme) is released into the small intestine in small, manageable amounts so that digestion can happen properly.

Ileocecal Sphincter (Ileocecal Valve)
Located where the small intestine ends and the large intestine (colon) begins. It is a one-way gate that allows digested material to pass from the small intestine into the large intestine, but prevents it from flowing backward.

Internal Anal Sphincter
This is involuntary — it stays contracted (closed) automatically all the time to prevent you from leaking stool without realizing it. It relaxes automatically when the rectum is full and ready for a bowel movement.

External Anal Sphincter
This is the voluntary one. This is the muscle you consciously squeeze to delay a bowel movement when you need to wait. It is the last gate before exit.

2. Urinary System

Internal Urethral Sphincter
Located at the base of the bladder where it connects to the urethra (the tube through which urine exits the body). It is involuntary and stays closed to prevent urine from leaking out continuously. It relaxes automatically when urination begins.

External Urethral Sphincter
This is voluntary. It lets you consciously delay urination when your bladder is full but you haven't reached a toilet yet. When you consciously "hold" your urine, this muscle is what you are tightening.

3. The Eye

Pupillary Sphincter (Sphincter Pupillae)
This is a tiny ring of muscle inside your eye that surrounds the pupil (the dark circular opening in the center). When light is bright, this sphincter contracts and makes the pupil smaller, reducing the amount of light entering the eye. In dim conditions, it relaxes and the pupil widens to let in more light. This happens automatically — you have no conscious control over it.

4. The Liver and Pancreas

Sphincter of Oddi
Located at the point where the bile duct and the pancreatic duct both empty into the small intestine. It controls the release of bile (from the liver and gallbladder) and digestive enzymes (from the pancreas) into the small intestine. It opens when food arrives in the small intestine, releasing these digestive fluids right when they are needed.

5. Blood Vessels

Precapillary Sphincters
These are microscopic sphincters found at the entrance to tiny blood vessels called capillaries. They regulate blood flow into specific tissues, directing more blood to areas that are active and need oxygen, and restricting flow to areas that are resting. For example, during exercise, precapillary sphincters in your leg muscles open up to allow more blood flow there.

Sphincters are essentially the body's traffic and flow management system. Without them, your body would have no ability to control the movement of substances from one compartment to another. Specifically, they:

  • Prevent backflow — stopping contents from moving in the wrong direction (like stomach acid going back into your esophagus).
  • Time the release of substances — ensuring digestive juices arrive exactly when food arrives, not before or after.
  • Maintain separation between body compartments — keeping the contents of one organ where they belong.
  • Allow conscious control over bodily functions — such as bowel and bladder control, which is fundamental to daily human functioning.
What Happens When a Sphincter Fails

A sphincter that is too loose, too tight, or damaged can cause serious medical problems:

  • A too-loose lower esophageal sphincter → chronic acid reflux and GERD (gastroesophageal reflux disease).
  • A too-tight pyloric sphincter in newborns → a condition called pyloric stenosis, where food cannot leave the stomach, causing forceful vomiting.
  • Damaged anal or urethral sphincters → incontinence (inability to control bowel movements or urination), which can result from injury, childbirth trauma, surgery, or neurological disease.
  • A blocked sphincter of Oddi → can trap bile or digestive enzymes and lead to pancreatitis (inflammation of the pancreas) or jaundice.

A sphincter is a circular ring muscle in the body that opens and closes a passage or opening — acting as a controlled biological gate — and they are found throughout the digestive, urinary, visual, and circulatory systems, where they regulate the flow of substances, prevent backflow, and maintain proper separation between the body's compartments.
14961: A sphinx is a mythological creature — meaning it exists in ancient stories and legends, not in real life. The classic sphinx has the body of a lion and the head of a human. Depending on the culture and tradition, it may also have wings. Think of it as a powerful, hybrid being that humans invented to represent something greater than an ordinary animal or a person alone.

The Greek Sphinx

In ancient Greek mythology, the Sphinx is a specific, famous monster. She has the head and chest of a woman, the body of a lion, and the wings of an eagle. She is not a gentle or decorative figure — she is dangerous and cunning.

According to the myth, the Sphinx sat at the entrance to the city of Thebes and stopped every traveler who passed by. She asked them a single riddle:

"What walks on four legs in the morning, two legs at noon, and three legs in the evening?"

If the traveler answered correctly, they could pass safely. If they got it wrong — she killed them. This went on, and many people died, until a man named Oedipus came along. He answered correctly: "Man" — a human being crawls on all fours as a baby (morning of life), walks on two legs as an adult (noon of life), and uses a walking stick (a "third leg") in old age (evening of life).

When Oedipus gave the right answer, the Sphinx, defeated, threw herself off a cliff and died.

This is why the Greek Sphinx is a symbol of a deadly puzzle — something that destroys those who cannot figure it out.

The Egyptian Sphinx

The Egyptian sphinx is quite different in feeling and purpose. In ancient Egypt, the sphinx was not a villain or a monster. It was a guardian — a powerful, protective symbol. Egyptian sphinxes typically have the body of a lion and the head of a pharaoh (the king), sometimes wearing the royal headdress. Occasionally, they have the head of a ram or a falcon instead of a human face, depending on which god they are associated with.

The most famous example in the world is the Great Sphinx of Giza, a massive statue carved directly out of limestone rock in Egypt, believed to be over 4,500 years old. It stands about 20 meters tall and 73 meters long — roughly as tall as a six-story building. It faces the rising sun, guarding the nearby pyramids. In ancient Egyptian belief, placing sphinxes at the entrance of temples and tombs was meant to ward off evil and protect what lay within.

So while the Greek sphinx asks a question and kills, the Egyptian sphinx watches in silence and guards.

The idea of a human-animal hybrid guardian or creature spread beyond Greece and Egypt. Sphinx-like creatures appear in the ancient art and mythology of Mesopotamia (modern-day Iraq), Persia (modern-day Iran), South Asia (India and Sri Lanka), and Southeast Asia. In many of these traditions, the creature carries similar symbolic weight — power, wisdom, and mystery. The specific features (wings, gender, type of animal body) vary, but the essential idea of a majestic, part-human, part-beast figure recurs across many civilizations independently.

Because the sphinx is associated with mystery, riddles, and hidden knowledge, the word moved into everyday language as a way to describe a person who is deeply mysterious and hard to read. If someone calls a person "a sphinx," or says they are "sphinx-like," they mean that person reveals very little about what they are thinking or feeling. They are quiet, unreadable, and perhaps secretive — you cannot figure out what is going on inside their head.

Example: "The old professor sat at the end of the table, a sphinx, giving nothing away with his expression."

This is one of the most common ways you will encounter the word in modern literature and conversation.

The word also gives its name to two real animals:

The Sphinx moth (also called a hawk moth) is a large, fast-flying moth that hovers in front of flowers to drink nectar, much like a hummingbird. It gets its name from the posture of its caterpillar, which rears up and holds its head high in a pose that reminded observers of the crouching Egyptian Sphinx.

The Sphynx cat (note the slight spelling variation) is a breed of domestic cat known for its almost complete lack of fur. It has a wrinkled, ancient-looking face that people felt resembled the stone face of the Great Sphinx of Giza — hence the name.

ContextWhat "sphinx" refers to

The word "sphinx" always carries the ideas of mystery, power, and a blend of human intelligence with animal strength. Whether it's the deadly riddle-keeper of Greek myth, the silent stone guardian of Egypt, the mysterious person who gives nothing away, or the moth and cat named after this ancient image — the word consistently evokes something ancient, formidable, and not entirely knowable. That is the soul of the word: something that sits at a threshold, between understanding and confusion, and dares you to figure it out.
14962:
A spice is a natural substance — almost always from a plant — that you add to food to give it a distinctive flavor, smell, or color. Spices make food taste richer, more interesting, and more complex. Without them, most food would taste flat and forgettable.

Think of it this way: if plain boiled rice is a blank canvas, a spice is what you use to paint something vivid and flavorful onto it.

Spices come from the harder, drier, or more concentrated parts of plants — not the soft leafy parts. Specifically:

  • Seeds — cumin, coriander, mustard seeds
  • Bark — cinnamon is literally the dried inner bark of a tree
  • Roots — ginger, turmeric
  • Berries — black pepper, allspice
  • Flower buds — cloves
  • The thread-like stigma of a flower — saffron, the world's most expensive spice

This is also what separates a spice from an herb. Herbs are the soft, green, leafy parts of plants — like basil, mint, or parsley. Spices are everything else: seeds, bark, roots, berries. A useful rule of thumb: if it's green and leafy, it's probably an herb; if it's a hard, dry, concentrated plant part, it's probably a spice.

A spice can do several jobs at once:

Flavor — This is the primary job. Every spice has a unique taste. Cinnamon is warm and sweet. Cumin is earthy and slightly smoky. Black pepper is sharp and biting. Cardamom is floral and almost perfume-like.

Aroma — Most spices smell as powerfully as they taste, and the smell often hits you before the taste does. Think of walking past a bakery using cinnamon, or a kitchen where cumin is being toasted.

Color — Some spices visually transform food. Turmeric turns food a vivid yellow. Paprika gives a deep red-orange tint. Saffron gives a rich golden color. This is why spices are sometimes used even when the flavor they add is subtle — the color alone is valuable.

Preservation — Before refrigerators existed, spices like cloves and cinnamon helped slow down the spoiling of food because of their natural antimicrobial properties. This is one reason spices were historically so precious.

"Spice" works both ways, and the meaning shifts slightly depending on how you use it.

As a countable noun — "a spice" or "spices" — you're referring to specific, individual types:

  • "Cinnamon is a spice."
  • "She bought five different spices at the market."
  • "Black pepper is the most widely used spice in the world."

As an uncountable noun — just "spice," no article, no plural — you're talking about it as a general concept, ingredient, or quality:

  • "This soup needs more spice." (= it needs more flavor/kick)
  • "Indian cooking uses a lot of spice."

In the uncountable form, you're not pointing to any one specific spice — you're talking about the idea of bold, aromatic flavoring in general.
Spices Range from Mild to Intense

It's worth knowing that not all spices are hot. People sometimes confuse "spicy" (meaning hot, like chili pepper) with the broader world of spices. But spices cover a huge range:

  • Sweet & warm — cinnamon, nutmeg, cloves
  • Earthy & smoky — cumin, smoked paprika
  • Floral & fragrant — cardamom, saffron, star anise
  • Sharp & hot — black pepper, chili, cayenne

So when someone says a dish "has a lot of spice," it doesn't necessarily mean it's hot — it could mean it's richly flavored with any combination of these.

"Spice" is also used beyond the kitchen. Figuratively, it means something that adds excitement, interest, or energy to something that might otherwise feel dull or flat.

This comes from the well-known saying: "Variety is the spice of life." Just as spices make food more enjoyable, variety — new experiences, different people, unexpected events — makes life feel richer and more engaging.

You'll hear it used like this:

  • "The surprise twist at the end gave the film a real spice." (= it made the film more exciting and alive)
  • "Her sharp wit adds spice to every conversation." (= makes it more interesting)
  • "Their routine had become too predictable — they needed some spice." (= excitement, freshness)

In this figurative sense, "spice" is almost always uncountable, and it carries the meaning of zest, vitality, or an engaging quality that elevates something ordinary.

• A spice rack — a small shelf or stand in a kitchen for storing jars of spices
  • A spice blend / spice mix — multiple spices combined into one mixture (e.g., curry powder, garam masala, five-spice powder)
  • A spice rub — a mixture of spices pressed onto meat before cooking to build a flavorful crust
  • "Variety is the spice of life" — the classic proverb meaning that doing different things keeps life interesting
  • The spice trade — the massive historical commerce in spices (pepper, nutmeg, cinnamon, cloves) that drove much of global exploration and shaped world history for centuries

Spice means a plant-based substance that flavors, colors, or aromas food — drawn from seeds, bark, roots, or other concentrated plant parts, never the green leafy portions. It can refer to a single specific type (a spice, spices) or to flavorful seasoning as a concept (spice in general). And beyond the kitchen, it stretches into everyday language to describe anything that makes a situation, story, or experience more vivid and alive.
14963: When you use "spice" as a verb, you are talking about adding something that makes a thing more flavorful, lively, or interesting — whether that thing is actual food, or something more abstract like a story, a relationship, or a routine. Think of it as injecting energy or excitement into something that feels plain or dull.

In its most direct sense, to spice something means to add spices — ingredients like pepper, chili, garlic, cinnamon, or cumin — to food in order to give it more flavor.

Examples:

  • "She spiced the soup with ginger and black pepper."
  • "The chef spiced the chicken well before grilling it."

Here, the action is physical and straightforward. You are seasoning food. The result is that the food goes from bland or plain to flavorful and rich.
The Figurative Meaning (The Far More Common Use)

This is where the verb really shines, and where you will encounter it most often in everyday English. In a figurative sense, to spice something (almost always paired with "up" — see below) means to make it more exciting, more interesting, more energetic, or more entertaining than it currently is.

The idea is borrowed directly from cooking. Just as a spice transforms a dull dish into something vibrant and enjoyable, you can "spice up" a situation to transform it from boring or stale into something that feels fresh and alive.

Examples:

  • "They decided to spice up their Friday nights by trying a new activity each week."
  • "The director spiced up the old script with some unexpected twists."
  • "He spiced up his presentation with funny stories and bold visuals."
  • "They wanted to spice up their relationship after years of the same routine."

Notice what is happening in each case. Something exists — a night, a script, a presentation, a relationship. It feels ordinary or predictable. Then someone deliberately adds something new — humor, surprise, novelty, creativity — to make it feel alive and engaging. That act of adding is "spicing up."

When used in the literal food sense, "spice" can stand alone perfectly fine:

  • "She spiced the rice." ✅

But in the figurative sense, you almost always need to include "up" to complete the meaning:

  • "Let's spice the evening." ❌ (sounds awkward or incomplete)
  • "Let's spice up the evening." ✅

The word "up" is not decorative here. It carries real meaning — it signals that you are elevating, intensifying, or improving something. Without it, the figurative meaning does not come through clearly.

You will also sometimes see "spice with" — even in figurative contexts — where the second part tells you what was used to add interest:

  • "She spiced her writing with dark humor."
  • "He spiced the lecture with surprising historical facts."

This construction is slightly more formal or literary, but it is correct and expressive.
What Kinds of Things Can Be "Spiced Up"?

Practically anything that can be described as dull, routine, flat, or predictable can be "spiced up." Here are the most common areas:

Relationships and social life — Couples spice up their romance. Friends spice up their hangouts. This suggests bringing in novelty, playfulness, or new experiences.

Work and creative projects — A writer spices up a boring report. A teacher spices up a lesson. A filmmaker spices up a sequel. This means adding creative elements — humor, drama, unexpected angles — that make the work more engaging.

Everyday routines — People spice up their diet, their workout, their commute, or their wardrobe. This means breaking the monotony with small changes that make things feel less predictable.

Conversation and communication — A speaker can spice up a speech with anecdotes, jokes, or dramatic pauses. A writer can spice up dialogue with wit and personality.
The Tone and Feel of the Word

"To spice (up)" is a warm, informal, and generally positive word. It carries a sense of fun and intentionality. When someone decides to spice something up, they are being proactive — they see dullness and they choose to fix it.

It is not a desperate or negative word. It does not imply that something was broken or failing. It simply implies that something good can be made even better, or something ordinary can be made memorable.

You would use this word comfortably in casual conversation, informal writing, and even in semi-professional contexts. It is rarely used in very formal or academic writing, where phrases like "enrich," "enliven," or "augment" might be preferred instead.

One subtle but important nuance: the word suggests a moderate, controlled addition of excitement — not an overwhelming transformation. Just as a chef adds spice carefully (too much ruins the dish), "spicing something up" implies thoughtful enhancement, not a dramatic overhaul.

If someone says "Let's spice up our road trip," they likely mean adding a fun detour, a playlist, or a game — not completely changing the destination. The original thing remains; it is simply made more vibrant.

To spice something means to add flavor — literally to food, and figuratively to any experience, piece of work, or routine. In figurative use, it almost always appears as "spice up," and it means to make something more lively, interesting, or exciting by introducing something new and stimulating into it. The word is positive, informal, and implies a deliberate, creative act of improvement.
14964:
A spiel is a long, smooth, rehearsed speech that someone delivers — usually to persuade you, sell you something, or get you to agree with them. The defining quality of a spiel is that it feels practiced. The person saying it has clearly said it many times before, and it flows out of them almost automatically.

Think of it like a script that someone has memorized and now delivers on demand.

Not every speech or explanation is a spiel. A spiel has a specific combination of qualities:

It is rehearsed. The speaker didn't just think of it now. They've said this exact thing — or something very close to it — many times before. It has a polished, well-oiled quality.

It is meant to persuade or convince. A spiel isn't just information. It's designed to get you on board with something — to buy a product, accept an idea, believe a story, or simply stop questioning.

It tends to be lengthy and flowing. A spiel isn't a quick one-liner. It's a full routine — thorough, detailed, and delivered without much pause or hesitation.

It often sounds slightly too smooth. This is the subtle part. Because a spiel is so rehearsed, it can feel a little mechanical or insincere — like the speaker is going through the motions rather than talking to you genuinely.
The Tone — Is It a Good or Bad Word?

"Spiel" sits somewhere between neutral and mildly negative in tone, depending on context.

When it is neutral: A waiter who has memorized the restaurant's daily specials and recites them to every table is giving a spiel. There's nothing wrong with it — it's just a practiced routine.

When it is negative: If a pushy salesperson corners you and launches into a long, over-rehearsed pitch full of flattery and pressure tactics, that's definitely a spiel — and the word used in this context carries a sense of skepticism or mild annoyance. The listener feels like they're being worked on rather than spoken to honestly.

So the word often suggests: "This person has said this a hundred times, and I'm not entirely sure how much of it is genuine."
Register — When Is This Word Used?

"Spiel" is an informal, everyday word. You'll hear it in casual conversation, not in formal writing or academic contexts. It belongs to the kind of language you'd use with a friend, not in a business report.

"Give someone a spiel" — to deliver your rehearsed speech to someone.
"The insurance agent gave me a spiel about all the reasons I needed extra coverage."

"Launch into a spiel" — to suddenly start delivering your spiel, often without much invitation.
"I asked one simple question, and he launched into a 10-minute spiel."

"The whole spiel" — the full, complete version of the rehearsed talk — nothing left out.
"She went through the whole spiel before I could even say anything."

"The usual spiel" — a spiel someone gives routinely, the same one they always use.
"He gave us the usual spiel about why our package was delayed."

Salespeople: This is the classic setting for a spiel. A car salesman who has a polished, well-practiced routine about why a particular car is the best value on the lot — hitting the same points, using the same phrases, every single time — is delivering a spiel.

Door-to-door sellers or telemarketers: These people have an actual script. When they call or knock, they go into their spiel immediately — often before you even have a chance to respond.

Someone making excuses: If a friend shows up late and immediately goes into a long, suspiciously smooth story about traffic, a phone call, a parking problem, and three other things — almost as if they had it prepared — you might think, "That sounds like quite the spiel."

Politicians: A politician who gives essentially the same speech at every event, hitting the same talking points in the same order with the same lines, is giving a spiel.

A tour guide: A guide who has memorized a detailed, flowing commentary about every landmark and delivers it the same way on every tour is working from a spiel — though in this case, the word would be used without any negativity.
How Spiel Differs From Similar Words

Speech is broad and neutral — any form of spoken address. A spiel is a specific kind of speech: rehearsed, persuasive, and often a little suspect.

Pitch is specifically about selling or proposing something. A spiel can overlap with a pitch, but a spiel is more about the manner (rehearsed, long, smooth) while a pitch is more about the goal (to sell or persuade).

Monologue just means one person is talking for a long time. A monologue has no implication of being rehearsed for the purpose of persuasion. A spiel does.

Lecture is educational and one-directional, but it carries authority and is usually sincere. A spiel can be insincere and is often self-serving.

A spiel is a smooth, rehearsed, often lengthy speech that someone delivers to persuade, impress, or win you over — practiced enough to feel like a routine, and sometimes smooth enough to make you a little suspicious.
14965: To spiel means to talk at length in a fast, smooth, and persuasive way — usually to sell something, convince someone, or impress them. Think of a street vendor who grabs your attention and launches into a non-stop, slick pitch about why you absolutely need what they're selling. That rapid, flowing, rehearsed-sounding talk? That's spieling.
What Makes It Different From Just "Talking"

Ordinary talking is neutral. Spieling has a specific flavour:

  • It is fast and fluent — the words roll out smoothly, without hesitation.
  • It feels rehearsed or well-practised — like the person has said it many times before.
  • It is aimed at persuading or impressing — there's always an angle or a goal behind it.
  • It often carries a slightly sceptical tone — the listener may sense that the speaker is being slick rather than fully genuine.

This is why "spiel" as a verb often carries a mildly negative or at least suspicious undertone. When you say someone is spieling, you're subtly hinting that their talk might be polished too well — that it's a performance as much as a conversation.

1. Spiel about something
This means to talk at length about a topic in that smooth, persuasive way.

"He spieled about the wonders of his new health supplement for twenty straight minutes."

2. Spiel off something
This means to rattle off a list or a set of information quickly and fluently — almost like reciting from memory.

"The waiter spieled off the day's specials so fast that nobody caught half of them."
"She spieled off a list of reasons why the project was delayed."
"Spiel" is an informal, colloquial word. You would use it in casual speech or informal writing, not in a formal essay or business report. It belongs to everyday language.

The word is most naturally associated with:

  • Salespeople making a pitch
  • Con artists or smooth-talkers trying to deceive
  • Showmen or entertainers drawing in a crowd
  • Anyone who launches into a long, practised-sounding speech when you just wanted a simple answer
The Feeling It Creates in the Listener

When someone spiels at you, you often feel like you're being talked to rather than spoken with. It's a one-way flow of words. You might find it impressive, exhausting, entertaining, or suspicious — but you rarely feel like you're having a genuine two-way conversation. That one-sided, monologue-like quality is central to what the verb captures.
A Simple Test to Know When to Use It

Ask yourself: Is this person talking fast and smoothly, with a clear goal of persuading or impressing, in a way that feels rehearsed or formulaic?

If yes — they are spieling.
14966: A spigot is a device that controls the flow of liquid — it lets you start, stop, or adjust how much liquid comes out of a pipe, a barrel, or any container holding fluid. Think of it as a "liquid gate": when you open it, liquid flows out; when you close it, it stops.
What It Looks Like and How It Works

A spigot typically has two parts working together:

  • A body — the main housing that is attached to the pipe or container.
  • A handle or knob — which you turn, twist, or push to open or close the flow.

When you rotate the handle, it moves an internal piece (a valve or plug) that either blocks the liquid's path or opens it up. It's a simple but powerful mechanism.

1. On the outside of a building (outdoor spigot)
This is probably the most common use of the word. If you've ever seen a metal faucet sticking out of an exterior wall of a house — where people connect a garden hose to water their lawn — that is a spigot. It is exposed to weather, usually made of brass or metal, and has a single handle you turn to release water.

2. On a barrel, keg, or large container
Before the age of modern plumbing, barrels were how people stored wine, beer, water, and oil. A spigot was the small tap inserted near the bottom of the barrel so you could draw the liquid out without opening the whole barrel. You'd push the spigot in, and liquid would flow into your cup. This is still common today — a wooden wine barrel at a winery, a beer keg at a party, or a large water dispenser at a campsite will often have a spigot at the bottom.

3. In a rain barrel or water collection system
Many people collect rainwater in large barrels placed under roof gutters. At the bottom of such a barrel, there is a spigot so you can drain the collected water into a watering can or hose.

4. In plumbing (a more technical meaning)
In professional plumbing, the word "spigot" has a specific technical meaning: it refers to the plain, smooth end of a pipe that is designed to slide into a wider, flared end (called the "socket" or "bell" end) of another pipe. This is called a spigot-and-socket joint. The two ends fit together like a hand going into a glove, and the joint is then sealed. This usage is common among plumbers and engineers working with drainage or sewer pipes. Here, the word "spigot" refers to a part of the pipe itself, not a valve.
Spigot vs. Faucet vs. Tap — What's the Difference?

These three words are closely related and are sometimes used interchangeably, but there are subtle differences worth knowing:

  • Faucet is used mainly in American English and typically refers to the fixtures inside a building — your kitchen sink faucet, your bathroom faucet. It tends to suggest a more finished, polished fixture.
  • Tap is the standard British English word for the same thing. In the UK, people say "turn on the tap," not "turn on the faucet."
  • Spigot in American English most naturally refers to an outdoor fixture or one on a container like a barrel. It has a rougher, more utilitarian feel. When someone says "the spigot in the backyard," they almost certainly mean the outdoor water valve on the exterior wall.

That said, in everyday casual speech, Americans often use "spigot" and "faucet" interchangeably for any kind of water valve, and this is perfectly acceptable.

Because a spigot controls whether something flows or stops, the word is widely used in a figurative sense to talk about anything that can be "turned on" or "turned off" like a flow:

  • "The government finally opened the spigot on disaster relief funding." — meaning: they started releasing money.
  • "They turned off the spigot on new hires." — meaning: they stopped hiring.
  • "His creativity flows like water from an open spigot." — meaning: his ideas come out easily and abundantly.

In all these cases, the spigot is used as a metaphor for a control point — the thing that determines whether a flow (of money, ideas, resources, information) is allowed or stopped.

• She walked to the side of the house and turned the spigot to fill the bucket.
  • The old wooden barrel had a brass spigot near its base.
  • He forgot to close the spigot after watering the garden, and water ran all night.
  • The plumber connected the spigot end of the new pipe into the socket of the old one.
  • Investors worried the company would turn off the spigot on research spending.

A spigot is a valve or tap — a device that opens and closes to control the flow of liquid from a pipe or container. You'll most commonly encounter the word when talking about outdoor water faucets on a house, taps on barrels or kegs, and in plumbing to describe the plain insertion end of a pipe. Figuratively, it means any controllable source or flow of something. It sits in the same family of words as faucet and tap, but carries a distinctly outdoor or utilitarian feel in American English.
14967:
A spike is a sharp, pointed object — like a thick, heavy nail, or the sharp tip of a fence. It stabs. It goes in fast and hard. It sticks out sharply.

Every meaning of the verb "to spike" traces back to this same feeling — something sharp, sudden, and forceful. Keep that image, and all the meanings below will click into place naturally.
1. The Literal Meaning: To Pierce or Impale

The most basic meaning is simply to stab or pin something using a sharp object.

"She spiked the receipt onto the metal stand on her desk."

Here, the action is exactly what it sounds like — a sharp object driven through something, holding it in place. Think of old-fashioned office "spike boards" where people would impale papers to file them.
2. To Put Spikes On Something

You can also spike something by attaching spikes to it — adding sharp points as part of its structure.

"The workers spiked the railway ties to the ground."
"He spiked his running shoes before the race."

The spiked shoes here are shoes with sharp studs added to the soles for grip. The workers drove large metal spikes (like nails) through wooden beams to hold the rails in place.
3. To Secretly Add Something to a Drink or Food

This is one of the most widely used meanings in everyday English. To spike a drink means to secretly add alcohol — or drugs — to someone's drink without their knowledge.

"Someone spiked the party punch with vodka."
"He didn't know his drink had been spiked."

The "spike" here is like a hidden jab — something is suddenly, unexpectedly inserted into the drink, just like a spike is thrust into something. The person drinking has no idea it's there. This meaning carries a strong sense of deception and surprise, and in serious cases, it describes a crime.

This idea also extends more loosely to food — where "spiking" means adding something potent to it, even openly:

"She spiked the salad dressing with a little chili oil."

Here the tone is not necessarily sinister — it just means something sharp and intense was added to lift the flavor.
4. To Increase Suddenly and Sharply

This is an extremely common meaning in news, finance, science, and everyday conversation. To spike means to shoot up suddenly to a much higher level — and usually just as quickly drop back down (though not always).

"Fuel prices spiked after the conflict began."
"Her temperature spiked in the middle of the night."
"Website traffic spiked after the article went viral."

Imagine a graph — a flat, calm line that suddenly shoots straight up into a sharp peak. That peak looks just like a spike. So when something "spikes," it means it rose sharply and dramatically in a short time.

You'll also see this used in reverse — a sudden sharp drop can sometimes be called a spike downward, though this is less common. The main usage is for a sudden upward surge.
5. To Kill or Suppress a Story (Journalism)

In the world of newspapers and journalism, to spike a story means to stop it from being published — to kill it, reject it, or bury it.

"The editor spiked the investigative piece at the last minute."
"The story was spiked after pressure from advertisers."

This comes directly from the literal spike: old newspaper offices kept a sharp metal spike on the editor's desk. Rejected articles were literally impaled on the spike — stabbed through — meaning they were dead and would never see print. Even though physical spikes are long gone, the word lives on. When a story is "spiked," it has been killed before the public ever sees it.
6. In Sports: To Hit the Ball Sharply Downward

In volleyball, to spike is one of the most exciting moves in the game. A player jumps up high and smashes the ball forcefully downward over the net, into the opponent's court — aiming for a sharp, fast, unstoppable hit.

"She jumped and spiked the ball right at the libero's feet."

The ball travels down like — you guessed it — a spike being driven into the ground.

In American football, a quarterback can "spike the ball" by slamming it into the ground immediately after the snap. This is done deliberately to stop the game clock.

"He spiked the ball with three seconds left to give the kicker time to set up."
7. To Spike Someone's Guns

This is an idiom — a fixed expression — that means to ruin someone's plans or prevent them from doing what they intended.

"Her sudden announcement spiked his plans to take credit for the project."
"They spiked his guns by releasing the report before he could."

Historically, soldiers would destroy a captured enemy cannon by hammering a metal spike into its firing hole, making it permanently useless. "Spiking the guns" meant the enemy's weapon was neutralized. Today, the idiom carries the same spirit — you've taken away someone's power to act.
8. In Science and Testing: To Add a Known Substance to a Sample

In chemistry, medicine, and research, to spike a sample means to deliberately add a known, measured amount of a substance to it — usually to test whether the testing method can detect and measure it accurately.

"The lab spiked the water sample with a small amount of lead to verify the test's accuracy."

This is a technical but important use. It's not secretive or harmful here — it's a controlled, intentional act. The "spike" is the added substance itself.
The Connecting Thread

Look back at everything above. Whether it's stabbing paper onto a metal stand, secretly adding something to a drink, a fever shooting up, or smashing a volleyball — every meaning of "spike" shares the same DNA:

Something sharp. Something sudden. Something forceful.

It either pierces (stabs into something), surges (shoots up sharply), kills (drives something dead), or hits hard and fast. That is the soul of this word.
A Quick Reference by Feel

If you feel…The meaning is…
Something was secretly added to a drinkSpiked (adulterated)
A number shot up suddenlySpiked (increased sharply)
A story was killed before publishingSpiked (suppressed)
A volleyball was smashed down hardSpiked (hit forcefully downward)
Someone's plan was ruinedSpiked their guns (idiom)
Something sharp was added for effectSpiked (intensified)

That is the verb "spike" — in every dimension it carries, with nothing left out.
14968: "Spiky" means having sharp points sticking outward. Think of a spike — a thin, rigid, sharply pointed object. When something is spiky, it has one or more of these sharp points, or it behaves like one. That image — a sharp point that can poke, pierce, or irritate — is the single thread connecting every meaning of this word.
Meaning 1: Literally Having Sharp Points (Physical Objects)

This is the most direct meaning. A physical object is spiky when it has sharp, pointed projections coming out of its surface.

Examples:

  • A cactus is spiky — its needles stick out and will poke you if you touch it.
  • A sea urchin is spiky — covered all over with sharp spines.
  • A pineapple's crown is spiky — those stiff, pointed leaves can scratch.
  • A fence made of iron spikes is spiky.
  • A hairbrush, a durian fruit, a thistle, a hedgehog's back — all spiky.

The key feeling: When something is spiky, you instinctively want to be careful around it. It signals don't touch or this will hurt.

What it is NOT: Something smooth, rounded, or soft is the opposite of spiky. A polished stone, a pillow, a peach — none of these are spiky. Spikiness requires those outward, sharp protrusions.

Degrees: Something can be mildly spiky (slightly rough to the touch, like a pinecone) or extremely spiky (like a metal spike strip that would flatten a car tire). The word covers the whole range.

This is a very common, everyday use. Hair is described as spiky when it stands up in stiff, sharp-looking points rather than lying flat or flowing softly. You've almost certainly seen this — hair that has been styled with gel or wax so that individual clumps or tips point upward or outward like little spikes.

Examples:

  • A punk rocker with a spiky mohawk.
  • A cartoon character whose hair sticks up in jagged points.
  • A child who just woke up with spiky bed-hair going in all directions.

This meaning is just an extension of Meaning 1 — the hair looks like spikes.
Meaning 3: A Person Who Is Easily Irritated or Difficult to Deal With

This is a figurative meaning — it's not about physical points at all. A spiky person is someone who is touchy, prickly, or easily offended. They react sharply or defensively, especially to criticism or challenges. Being around them feels a little like being near that cactus — you have to be careful what you say, or you'll get "poked."

Examples:

  • "He gets very spiky when anyone questions his decisions." — He reacts badly; he snaps, gets defensive, or takes offense quickly.
  • "She's a bit spiky with strangers, but warm once she knows you." — She comes across as cold, guarded, or sharp-edged at first.
  • "The meeting turned spiky when salaries came up." — The mood became tense and uncomfortable, with people speaking sharply to each other.

The connection to Meaning 1: Just as a physical spike warns stay away, a spiky person's sharp reactions send the same social signal — tread carefully here. The word carries the same sense of unpredictable sharpness that can hurt you.

Important nuance: A spiky person is not necessarily cruel or aggressive. They're just easily pricked themselves — sensitive in a way that makes them lash out. It's more like defensiveness than malice.
Meaning 4: Sharp, Pointed, and Provocative in Communication or Style

Writing, humor, commentary, or debate can be called spiky when it is sharp, pointed, and deliberately edgy — designed to challenge, provoke thought, or cut through vague, polite language. It's not gentle or diplomatic. It has bite.

Examples:

  • "Her spiky column in the newspaper ruffled a lot of feathers." — The article was bold, direct, and deliberately provocative.
  • "He's known for his spiky wit." — His humor is clever but sharp; it might sting a little.
  • "The debate took a spiky turn when the candidates stopped being polite." — The conversation became pointed and combative.

The connection to Meaning 1: A spiky argument or a spiky piece of writing pokes at ideas, assumptions, or people. It doesn't let things slide smoothly by — it catches on things, like a spike would.

What it is NOT: The opposite of spiky writing is smooth, bland, safe, or diplomatic writing — the kind that avoids sharp edges and says nothing that could poke anyone.
Meaning 5: Sharp, Sudden Ups and Downs in Data or Patterns

In contexts like graphs, statistics, economic data, or performance metrics, spiky describes a pattern that is volatile and jagged — with sudden, sharp rises and drops — rather than smooth and gradual.

Examples:

  • "The website's traffic was spiky — millions of visitors one day, almost none the next."
  • "Energy demand in a city is spiky: it surges during the morning rush and drops at night."
  • "The graph of his heart rate was spiky during the race."

If you imagine drawing a line on a graph, a smooth line curves gently. A spiky line shoots suddenly up, then drops sharply — like mountain peaks and valleys, one after another. Each peak looks like a spike.

The connection to Meaning 1: The shape of the data looks like spikes on a graph. The word is borrowed directly from the visual image.

Every meaning of "spiky" shares the same core character: sharpness that protrudes outward and demands attention. Whether it's a cactus needle, a person who snaps when challenged, a bold opinion that pokes at comfortable ideas, or a line on a graph that shoots up and down — something spiky is never soft, smooth, or easily ignored. It has edges. It points at you.

Sharp — "sharp" is broader and more neutral. A sharp knife, a sharp mind, a sharp turn. "Spiky" adds the sense of multiple pointed projections, or a specifically prickly, guarded quality in personality.

Prickly — Very close in meaning, especially for personality (Meaning 3). "Prickly" leans slightly more toward a person being sensitive and defensive. "Spiky" can feel slightly more aggressive in its sharpness. They are often interchangeable.

Jagged — Similar to "spiky" for physical objects and data, but "jagged" suggests uneven, broken edges (like shattered glass), while "spiky" specifically suggests distinct, pointed projections sticking out.

Edgy — Similar to "spiky" in communication (Meaning 4), but "edgy" often implies something that pushes against social norms or causes discomfort. "Spiky" focuses more on sharpness and directness of expression.

ContextWhat "spiky" means

In short: if something is spiky, it has sharp points — real ones you can touch, or metaphorical ones you can feel. Physical things poke you. Spiky people poke back when touched. Spiky ideas poke at assumptions. Spiky data pokes up and down on a graph. The sharpness, the protrusion, and the slight sense of be careful — that is "spiky."
14969: At the heart of "spin" is one simple image: rotation. Something turning around and around a central point. Almost every meaning of this word connects back to that image — either literally (physical rotation) or as a metaphor (something that extends, twists, or turns in a figurative sense).
Meaning 1: To Rotate Rapidly

The most direct meaning. When something spins, it turns in circles around a fixed center point, usually quickly.

The Earth spins on its axis once every 24 hours.
He spun the bottle and watched it twirl on the table.
The wheel spun faster and faster.

One important note: when something spins on a point, it stays in one place while rotating. A spinning top spins — it rotates without going anywhere. This is different from revolving or orbiting, which involves moving around something else (the Earth revolves around the Sun, but it spins on its own axis).
Meaning 2: To Turn Around Quickly

You can spin yourself (turn your whole body around fast), or spin something else (throw or move it in a way that causes rotation).

She spun around when she heard her name.
He spun his keys on his finger.
The batsman spun to face the new delivery.
Meaning 3: To Make Thread or Yarn

Before machines did it, people made thread by pulling out raw fibers — wool, cotton, flax — and twisting them tightly together. This process is called spinning. The traditional device for it is a spinning wheel.

She spun wool every evening by the firelight.
The villagers spun their own cloth before the mills arrived.

Spiders use this same word: they spin their webs — drawing silk out of their bodies and shaping it into a structure.

The spider spun a perfect web in the corner of the window.

The connection to rotation is clear: spinning thread involves continuously twisting fibers in a circular motion.
Meaning 4: To Feel Dizzy or Overwhelmed

When your head spins, you feel as if the room (or the world) is rotating around you — that classic sense of dizziness. It's used both literally and figuratively.

Literal (actual physical dizziness):

After spinning in circles, the kids fell over laughing — their heads were spinning.

Figurative (mentally overwhelmed, confused, or excited to the point of disorientation):

The sheer number of choices made my head spin.
When she heard she'd won the prize, her head spun with disbelief.

The figurative use is very common. It captures the feeling of being so flooded with information, emotion, or stimulation that your mind can't quite keep up.
Meaning 5: To Present Information With a Bias

This is one of the most important modern meanings of the word, especially in journalism and politics.

To spin information means to present it in a deliberately selective or framed way — not outright lying, but choosing which facts to highlight, which to downplay, and how to word things, so that the audience forms a particular impression that suits your agenda.

After the disaster, the company spun the story as an "isolated incident" with no systemic problems.
Both sides were busy spinning the election results to their advantage.
Don't be fooled — that press release is pure spin.

A person whose professional job is to do this is called a spin doctor — typically someone hired by a politician or corporation to manage public perception.

The connection to the core idea of "spin" is poetic: just as putting spin on a ball changes its trajectory without changing the ball itself, putting spin on a story changes how people perceive it without changing the underlying facts.
Meaning 6: To Tell an Elaborate or Drawn-Out Story

To spin a yarn or spin a tale means to tell a story — typically a long, vivid, entertaining one, often with exaggeration, embellishment, or details that may not be entirely truthful.

The old sailor spun yarns about sea monsters and buried treasure.
She spun a tale so convincing that everyone believed her.

The phrase comes from the idea of spinning thread — drawing something out at length, pulling it longer and longer. A good storyteller "draws out" a narrative the same way a spinner draws out thread.

You can also use "spin" without "yarn" or "tale" in the same sense:

He spun a whole elaborate story about why he was late.

The implication is usually that the story is imaginative, possibly exaggerated, and maybe not entirely trustworthy.
Meaning 7: To Move or Drive Quickly (Informal)

In casual, informal speech — especially British English — spin can mean to travel or drive somewhere quickly, usually for a short distance or on a quick errand.

Let's spin around the block and see how the new car feels.
She spun over to the shop and was back in ten minutes.
Meaning 8: To Skid Out of Control (Vehicle)

When a vehicle spins or spins out, it loses traction — usually on ice, gravel, or wet road — and rotates uncontrollably, often swerving dangerously.

He braked too hard on the ice, and the car spun out.
The racing driver's car spun off the track after the collision.

This is very directly connected to the physical meaning: the vehicle literally starts rotating where it shouldn't.
Meaning 9: To Prolong or Draw Something Out Unnecessarily

To spin something out means to extend it far longer than necessary — to stretch it out artificially, often to waste time or avoid reaching a conclusion.

He spun the meeting out for two hours with pointless questions.
She spun the negotiations out for months, hoping for a better offer.

Again, notice the thread-spinning image underneath: drawing something out slowly and at length.
Meaning 10: To Create a New Thing From an Existing One (Spin Off)

To spin off means to create a new, separate entity that branches out from something that already exists. A company might spin off one of its divisions as an independent business. A popular TV show might spin off a new series focused on one of its characters.

The tech giant spun off its cloud division as a separate company.
The show was so successful it spun off three new series.

The resulting thing is called a spin-off (noun). The idea is that something is "spun out" from the original, like thread pulled from a spool.
All Meanings at a Glance

Here is every meaning, in plain words:

  1. To rotate rapidly — a wheel, a top, the Earth spinning on its axis
  2. To turn quickly — spinning around to face someone, spinning a ball
  3. To make thread — by twisting fibers; also what spiders do with silk
  4. To feel dizzy or overwhelmed — "my head is spinning"
  5. To put a biased angle on information — politicians and PR people spin stories
  6. To tell an elaborate story — "spin a yarn," often with exaggeration
  7. To travel somewhere quickly (informal) — "spin around the block"
  8. To lose control and skid (vehicle) — "spin out" on ice
  9. To draw something out too long — spinning out a meeting, a speech, negotiations
  10. To create a new entity from an existing one — spin off a company or TV show
Key Phrases You Will Encounter

Spin a yarn / spin a tale — to tell a long, often exaggerated story

He spun a yarn about fighting a lion with his bare hands.

Spin out — (1) a vehicle loses control and rotates (2) a person becomes overwhelmed or panicked (3) to extend something too long

I was spinning out about the exam. (= overwhelmed, panicking)

Spin off — to create something new from something existing

The research spun off a whole new industry.

Head is spinning — feeling dizzy or overwhelmed

After three hours of data, my head was spinning.

Spin doctor — a professional who manages and shapes public perception of events

The politician brought in a spin doctor to handle the press.

Put a spin on something — to present something with a particular angle or bias

The journalist accused the company of putting a positive spin on its losses.
The Unifying Thread

Every meaning of "spin" comes back to some version of the same idea: circular motion, extension, or turning something in a direction it wouldn't naturally go. Physical spinning (a wheel, a top) is the root. From there, the word extends to making thread (which involves twisting in circles), to feeling dizzy (a sensation of spinning), to drawing out a story or a meeting (pulling it long, like thread), to biasing information (putting a "turn" on it), to creating spin-offs (things that branch out like thread from a spindle).

Once you see that core image, all the meanings click into place naturally.
